entries.title: Getting started with Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
entries.summary: Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore returns a synthesized, source-cited answer to a natural-language question in a single tool call, with no search, retrieve, synthesize, and citation pipeline to build. Learn how it works and how to add it to an AgentCore Gateway and call it from an agent.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Getting started with Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

Today, we are announcing the general availability of Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. With Web Answer, agent builders get a synthesized, source-cited answer to a natural-language question with a single tool call. They no longer build a search, retrieve, synthesize, and citation pipeline themselves.

If you have built agents that need to answer questions from current web sources, you know the pattern: call a search API, decide which results to trust, retrieve and clean page content, prompt a model to synthesize, and engineer citation extraction so the output traces back to a source. Every step is code you maintain, and every step is another place things can go wrong: hallucination when evidence is insufficient, stale content when the index moves, and broken attribution when a claim and its source drift apart.

The Web Answer collapses that entire pipeline into one request. You send a question. You get back a cited answer in seconds. In this post, we explain what Web Answer does, compare it with Web Search on AgentCore, show how it works and what it returns, and walk through adding Web Answer to a gateway and calling it from an agent.

What Web Answer does

Your agent sends a question to your AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The Gateway authenticates the call with AWS Identity and Access Management (AWS IAM) or a JSON Web Token (JWT). The Gateway calls Web Answer, a managed connector that AWS owns, using its own service role. Web Answer plans its searches, runs several in parallel, and reads key pages to check the facts. When the evidence is insufficient, it searches again. It then writes an answer that ties each claim to its source URL. The Gateway returns the answer and its citations to your agent as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool result.

Web Answer is a managed AgentCore Gateway tool that takes a natural-language question and returns a synthesized answer in seconds grounded in current web sources. Here is what you get back:

  • A grounded, cited answer, where each grounded claim maps to a citation, with a source URL where one is available.
  • Current sources. Web Answer runs new searches for every question, and its model is given today’s date so it can search for up-to-date information.
  • Agentic search: Web Answer plans its own searches, runs several in parallel, reads pages to verify facts, and decides when it has enough evidence to answer.
  • Responsible AI safeguards: Web Answer is designed and tested with responsible AI safeguards.

Figure 2: Demo video showing how to add Web Answer to an AgentCore Gateway, from setup to a finished, cited answer

How it differs from Web Search

Web Answer and the Web Search tools both support retrieval use cases, with different levels of integration complexity. The dividing line is who runs the model:

  • Web Search: Returns ranked URLs, titles, snippets, and metadata. You keep your own model and control the synthesis. Use Web Search when you want full control over how results are processed.
  • Web Answer: Runs the model, the agentic retrieval loop, synthesis, and attribution for you. You get a finished, cited answer. Use Web Answer when the question is a sub-task inside a larger agent and you do not want to own a retrieval pipeline for it.

Many customers will use both. An agent might use Web Search for broad research tasks where it needs raw results, and Web Answer for specific factual questions where it needs a quick, cited answer.

Set up and invoke Web Answer

Web Answer is a connector that AWS owns. You reference it by ID, and the Gateway handles the tool schema, parameter governance, endpoint resolution, and authentication to the backend. In this walkthrough, you give your Gateway’s service role permission to call Web Answer, add a Web Answer target, and call it from a Strands agent.

Getting started

Getting started takes minutes. A Gateway administrator adds Web Answer as a target on an existing AgentCore Gateway, and the tool appears to any attached agent over MCP through 

tools/list
and 
tools/call
.

Prerequisites

  • An AWS account with AgentCore Gateway access.
  • An AgentCore Gateway in us-east-1 that uses IAM (
    AWS_IAM
    ) inbound authentication. To create one, see Create an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway in the Developer Guide.
  • AWS credentials for an identity that has 
    bedrock-agentcore:InvokeGateway
    on the Gateway, and Amazon Bedrock access to the model your agent uses.
  • Python 3.10 or later, with the required packages:

Note: Following these steps creates AWS resources that incur charges. The Gateway and Web Answer invocations are billable. See the Pricing section that follows for details, and when you finish, delete the resources you created (see “Clean up resources”).

Step 1: Grant the Gateway service role access to Web Answer

The Gateway uses its service role to act on your behalf. The role’s trust policy allows 

bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com
to assume it, scoped to your account. For Web Answer, the role needs:
  • bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebAnswer
    , to call Web Answer. The Gateway checks this permission on every request against the ARN that AWS owns, 
    arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-east-1:aws:tool/web-answer.v1
    .

Attach the policy to the service role as an inline policy:

The role controls only the Gateway’s outbound calls. Who can call your Gateway is set by its inbound authorizer. The role also doesn’t need 

bedrock:InvokeModel
: your agent’s model runs under your agent’s own identity.

Step 2: Create the Web Answer target

Add Web Answer as a connector target. The 

connectorId
tells the Gateway which managed integration to provision: in this case, an agent that searches the web and writes a cited answer.

Outbound authentication is automatic for connectors. With 

GATEWAY_IAM_ROLE
, the Gateway calls the Web Answer backend with the service role from Step 1, so you don’t create or store any credentials for the tool. Wait until 
get_gateway_target
reports the target status as 
READY
before you call it.

As the Gateway administrator, you can also set a domain filter on the target. The filter applies to every call that goes through the target. To limit the target to a set of domains, set 

parameterValues
to 
{"domainFilter": {"include": ["bis.org"], "exclude": ["unreliable-source.net"]}}
.

Step 3: Invoke Web Answer from a Strands agent

Your agent discovers Web Answer through the Gateway’s 

tools/list
and calls it with 
tools/call
, like any other MCP tool. This works with Strands Agents, LangChain, LangGraph, CrewAI, or any other MCP-compatible client.

When a question needs current information, your agent calls the Web Answer tool (

web-answer-tool___WebAnswer
). Web Answer runs the agentic search and returns a finished answer with citations.

Besides the question, the Web Answer tool takes optional arguments that your agent can set on each call: a domain filter to include or exclude sites, a published-date range, and a country to localize results. The agent’s domain filter is combined with the target’s filter. The agent can exclude more domains, or limit results to some of the target’s included domains, but it can’t add a domain that the target’s filter blocks.

Response format

Web Answer returns an MCP tool result with both content and structuredContent fields. The answer is markdown text with inline citation markers like [1], and structuredContent.answer carries the same text alongside a structured citations list:

structuredContent.answer normally holds a single block. Each citation carries the source url and, when available, the domain.

Clean up resources

Delete the Web Answer target when you no longer need it:

If you created the Gateway only for this walkthrough, delete its targets first, then the Gateway (delete_gateway), and then the service role and its policy. There is no persistent infrastructure on the AWS side beyond these resources. After they are removed, you stop incurring charges.

Enterprise controls, built in

Web Answer inherits the same enterprise controls as other AgentCore tools:

  • Gateway authentication. No separate API key to provision, rotate, or manage for Web Answer. Callers authenticate to the gateway with the inbound method you configure, such as AWS IAM (SigV4) or a JSON Web Token from your identity provider. The gateway then calls Web Answer with its own service role, which needs the 
    bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebAnswer
    permission.
  • VPC and AWS PrivateLink. Your agents can call the gateway through an interface virtual private cloud (VPC) endpoint (
    com.amazonaws.us-east-1.bedrock-agentcore.gateway
    ), so traffic stays off the public internet.
  • Zero data egress. Your queries and results stay within your AWS environment.
  • Amazon CloudWatch metrics. Operational metrics publish to CloudWatch from the first call.
  • Per-account rate limits. Enforced from launch, with 10 transactions per second per account in US East (N. Virginia) (us-east-1). To request an increase, contact AWS Support.
  • Admin-time policy bounds. The Gateway administrator sets domain filter bounds at target setup. Agents can narrow the filter bounds on each call but can’t widen them.
  • Queries stay within AWS. Web Answer searches an Amazon-operated web index and Amazon’s knowledge graph, and doesn’t send your question to third-party search engines or external websites.

Use cases

Web Answer helps agents retrieve current, cited information to support a range of knowledge-intensive workflows. Example scenarios include:

  • Financial services. Regulatory Q&A agents answering questions about compliance requirements, market regulations, and policy changes, where every answer must trace to an authoritative source.
  • Healthcare. Clinical support agents grounding responses in current medical literature and treatment guidelines published on the web.
  • Customer service. Support agents answering product and policy questions in real time, where ten ranked links are not useful and a cited answer is.
  • Legal and compliance. Research assistants answering questions about case law, regulatory filings, and policy interpretations with auditable citations.
  • Enterprise knowledge workers. Internal copilots that answer questions from current public information without requiring employees to build their own search and synthesis workflow.

Availability

Web Answer is available in US East (N. Virginia) (us-east-1), with more AWS Regions coming soon.

Pricing

Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is priced at $10 per 1,000 tool calls.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed how Web Answer gives your agents current, cited answers through agentic search, with no search pipeline for you to build or maintain. We granted a Gateway service role access to Web Answer, added a Web Answer target, called it from a Strands agent, and read the answer and its citations from the response. Use Web Search on AgentCore when your own model should reason over raw results, and Web Answer when your agent needs a finished, cited answer.

To get started, see:

  • Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation
  • Web Answer structured output schema
  • Adding Web Answer to an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway
  • Supported regions

entries.title: How Amazon Marketplace evaluates content quality with Amazon SageMaker AI
entries.summary: Learn how Amazon Marketplace evaluates A+ Content quality at scale on Amazon SageMaker AI by rendering each product page as a single snapshot, scoring it with a vision-language model fused with OCR readability signals in a CatBoost classifier, and using SHAP to turn each decision into prioritized, actionable recommendations for selling partners.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

How Amazon Marketplace evaluates content quality with Amazon SageMaker AI

A+ Content is the rich media widget on the Amazon product detail page. Through visual assets, brands communicate unique product and brand value to help customers make informed purchase decisions. Selling partners using high-quality A+ Content boost their sales by 8–20 percent compared to those without it. A wide variety of brands, from established brands with large in-house design teams to bootstrapped brands with limited resources, use A+ Content, creating inconsistency in content quality. A typical A+ Content project combines text, images, and video into a cohesive product story. Evaluating each asset in isolation misses the quality that emerges from how those assets work together. When your content spans multiple heterogeneous modules and you need a holistic quality signal rather than per-asset checks, the multi-model fusion approach described in this post can help. In this post, we examine this problem in the context of A+ Content.

A+ Content provides creative freedom for selling partners to express their authentic selves on their product detail pages, without strict content specifications such as image ratio and text word count.

Although this flexibility allows compelling brand storytelling, it also creates substantial variation in content composition and quality.

With quality evaluation and improvement recommendations, brands can transform average content into high-quality content that is more coherent, relevant, and useful. This improved content helps customers make more informed purchasing decisions and build lasting relationships with brands, leading to improved revenue for selling partners.

To achieve this goal, an evaluation system must assess the complete content experience, provide actionable recommendations beyond numeric scores, and reflect the nuances across product categories. Existing approaches struggle to meet all these requirements simultaneously, so in this post, you will see a new approach using Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to understand and evaluate content holistically, and a diffusion-based generation component that produces improved visual assets from the resulting quality signals.

In this post, you will learn how to:

  • Render complete ecommerce content as a single snapshot and evaluate it holistically with a VLM.
  • Combine VLM semantic scores with OCR readability signals in a lightweight CatBoost classifier trained on expert annotations.
  • Use SHAP to explain quality decisions and generate actionable improvement recommendations for selling partners.
  • Implement the end-to-end pipeline on Amazon SageMaker AI, from data ingestion and annotation through model hosting, explainability, and production monitoring.

Opportunities and challenges in VLM-based evaluation

A vision language model (VLM) pairs an image encoder with a large language model (LLM). The encoder, often a vision transformer (ViT), splits an image into patches and turns them into embeddings, and a small connector maps those embeddings into the language model’s input space (Flamingo, LLaVA). Many VLMs reuse the image encoder from CLIP, which learned to match images with their captions. Because VLMs are trained to follow instructions, you can give one an image along with a rubric of evaluation criteria and get back a written assessment without task-specific training. When you need closer agreement with human reviewers, you can fine-tune the model on labeled examples. This makes VLMs a practical starting point for checking product images against your content guidelines at scale.

Conventional computer vision models can already score individual assets, for example flagging a blurry image or a grammar error in a bullet list. Using a VLM to grade each asset separately adds little beyond that. A product detail page, however, combines images, text, and layout modules into a single story, and its quality depends on how those pieces work together. Our approach renders the full page as a single snapshot and asks the VLM to evaluate it as customers see it.

Consider a blender page with a hero image, a bulleted feature list highlighting blade speed and capacity, and a lifestyle photo of the blender in a modern kitchen. Checked one by one, each asset passes: the image is sharp, the bullets are grammatical, and the photo is well lit. Viewed together, problems appear. The bullets might advertise a 64-oz pitcher while the lifestyle photo shows a single-serve model, or the lifestyle photo might sit above the hero image so customers see the kitchen before the product. Because an asset’s meaning depends on where it appears and what surrounds it, these issues only show up when the page is evaluated as a whole. The snapshot gives the VLM that complete view. Using it in production adds three requirements: scores must match expert quality standards, evaluation must be accurate and efficient at scale, and each result must explain what to fix.

As shown in Figure 1, we address these considerations through a VLM-based multi-model fusion architecture designed around adaptability, performance, and explainability. The following sections describe each component.

Adaptive VLM content evaluation with expert annotations

A pretrained VLM prompted with a rubric scores content from its general knowledge, and those scores don’t always match ecommerce quality standards. Fine-tuning the VLM to close that gap would require GPU training infrastructure and, with only a few thousand labeled examples, carries a real risk of overfitting. Instead, we keep the VLM and rubric prompt fixed, use the VLM’s structured outputs as features, and train a CatBoost classifier on them to predict expert quality labels. CatBoost, a gradient-boosted decision tree library, performs well on small tabular datasets like this one. Because only the classifier is retrained, updating the system as annotations accumulate or criteria change takes a short CPU-only job rather than a foundation model fine-tuning run.

The VLM receives the page snapshot and a rubric prompt covering four quality dimensions: Visual Storytelling, Feature Presentation, A+ Layout, and Conversion Optimization. Each dimension has explicit criteria and point-deduction rules. For each dimension, the VLM returns a score from 0 to 10, a confidence value, and a natural-language rationale. For example, it lowers the score and explains why when a page lacks diverse modules or lifestyle imagery, or repeats information. The scores and confidence values become the classifier’s features, and the rationales help selling partners understand the result.

To build the training labels, one ecommerce marketing expert and four professional annotators independently rated 5,478 product detail pages from 10 product categories as high or low quality, using the same criteria. We assessed their ratings and took the majority vote to create a consensus label. The classes are nearly balanced (49.6 percent high quality), so a classifier can’t score well by predicting the majority class. To measure label reliability, we used Cohen’s kappa, which measures how often two raters agree after accounting for the agreement they would reach by chance. A score of 0 means agreement is no better than chance, 1 means perfect agreement, and values above 0.8 are generally considered strong. Each annotator scored between 0.845 and 0.915 when compared against the consensus label.

We compared the classifier with a baseline on a 20 percent holdout set (about 1,100 pages). The baseline averages the four VLM scores and applies a fixed threshold, so every dimension counts equally. The baseline reached 0.80 accuracy and an F1 score of 0.84 on the high-quality class. The CatBoost classifier, trained on the same scores, reached 0.89 accuracy and an F1 score of 0.90. Because the classifier learns how much each dimension matters and how the dimensions interact, its predictions match expert decisions more closely.

High-performance VLM content evaluation with OCR

VLMs capture the overall meaning and visual composition of a page well, but they are less reliable at fine-grained readability issues, such as how crowded the text is or how much space separates lines. Because of their language-model foundation, they can also favor long, detailed descriptions even when customers prefer concise text they can scan quickly. On a text-heavy page, a VLM might rate dense product information as helpful while customers struggle to read long sentences packed into a small area. To capture these issues, we use an optical character recognition (OCR) model hosted on SageMaker AI Inference to extract each block of text and its position, then calculate four quantitative signals: Text Density, Character Density, Spacing, and Overall Readability. Combining these OCR scores with the VLM’s semantic and visual assessment adds complementary information that improves quality classification.

From that output, we calculate four readability scores:

  • Text Density: The share of the page area covered by text.
  • Character Density: The number of characters per unit of page area.
  • Spacing: How consistent and sufficient the whitespace is between words, lines, and paragraphs.
  • Overall Readability: A combined signal from the three preceding scores.

Because these scores depend on layout rather than wording, two pages with identical text can score differently.

The fusion model combines the four VLM rubric scores and the four OCR scores into eight features and trains a CatBoost classifier on the same expert labels. Table 1 compares it with models trained on each feature set alone, using the same 20 percent holdout set.

On the same 20 percent holdout set, the CatBoost model using only OCR features achieved 0.82 accuracy and a 0.83 F1 score, while the model using only VLM features achieved 0.89 and 0.90. The fused 

OCR-VLM-CatBoost
model outperformed both standalone models, reaching 0.94 accuracy and a 0.95 F1 score. The 0.05 improvement in both metrics over the VLM-only model demonstrates that OCR isn’t a replacement signal. It complements the VLM’s holistic judgment with fine-grained text-readability information.
ConfigurationAccuracyF1 Score
Baseline (averaged VLM scores + threshold)0.800.84
OCR-only CatBoost0.820.83
VLM-only CatBoost0.890.90
Fused OCR-VLM CatBoost0.940.95

Explainable VLM content evaluation with SHAP

A quality label alone doesn’t tell selling partners what to fix first. To find which dimensions drove each decision, we use SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), which assigns each feature a value showing how far it pushed a prediction toward high or low quality. Because the VLM and OCR scores feed the same classifier, SHAP measures both on a common scale. Raw scores can’t do this: a Visual Storytelling score of 6 and a high Character Density don’t tell you which one mattered more to the decision.

Across the holdout set, the most influential features were OCR Character Density (mean absolute SHAP value 1.1), OCR Overall Readability (1.0), and VLM Visual Storytelling (1.0). They were followed by A+ Layout (0.8), Feature Presentation (0.6), and Conversion Optimization (0.4). Both OCR and VLM features rank near the top, so the classifier depends on both sources.

For an individual page, SHAP shows which features lowered the decision. For each page classified as low quality, we rank the eight features by SHAP value, then pass the most negative features, the product category, and ecommerce best practices, along with the VLM’s rationales, to an LLM, which turns them into prioritized, specific actions.

Figure 4 shows two local SHAP plots with the LLM reasoning grounded in the SHAP results, for a low-quality and a high-quality A+ Content sample. For example, if A+ Layout has a SHAP value of -1.2 and Visual Storytelling has -0.3, the system prioritizes restructuring the layout and rebalancing text and images, followed by improvements to the imagery.

Figure 4: Two local SHAP value distributions for all VLM and OCR features: (a) a low-quality case, where most features contribute negatively and drive an improvement-requested recommendation; (b) a high-quality case, where most features contribute positively

We validated the effectiveness of these explanation-based recommendations by measuring quality scores after selling partners revised their content. The average post-revision quality score increased by 1.4 points on a 10-point scale on a statistically significant sample. SHAP contributions can therefore be translated from decision explanations into actionable improvement priorities and methods. Explainability is therefore not merely an auxiliary capability for understanding the model. It functions as a feedback mechanism that materially improves content quality.

Results

The complete system scores each page snapshot with the VLM and OCR, combines the four VLM scores and four OCR scores into a single feature vector, and passes it to a CatBoost classifier trained on expert labels. SHAP then identifies which features drove each decision. To measure what each component adds, we compared four configurations on the same 20 percent holdout set. The holdout set comes from 5,478 product detail pages across 10 product categories, including Furniture, Shoes, Grocery, Beauty, and Apparel.

The baseline averages the four VLM scores and applies a fixed threshold, so every dimension counts equally. It reached 0.80 accuracy and an F1 score of 0.84. Training a CatBoost classifier on the same scores lets the model learn which dimensions matter most and how they interact, which raised accuracy to 0.89 and F1 to 0.90. A classifier trained on the OCR scores alone reached 0.82 accuracy and an F1 score of 0.83. Combining the VLM and OCR scores gave the best results, with 0.94 accuracy and an F1 score of 0.95. That’s 14 percentage points higher accuracy and 11 points higher F1 than the baseline.

Examining each performance gain separately makes the value of the integrated approach clearer. CatBoost calibration first reduces the limitations of a fixed threshold by learning dimension-specific weights and nonlinear decision boundaries. Adding OCR features then supplies text-readability signals that the VLM can miss. Overall, the final fusion model improves accuracy by 0.14 and F1 by 0.11 over the baseline.

We also changed the VLM backbone in an additional experiment on a single-category dataset containing 499 content projects. With a lighter VLM variant, the baseline achieved 0.74 accuracy and a 0.72 F1 score, while the 

OCR-VLM-CatBoost
model achieved 0.90 for both metrics. With a more capable VLM variant, the baseline achieved 0.79 accuracy and a 0.84 F1 score, while the fusion model achieved 0.94 and 0.95. The fusion approach improved accuracy by 0.16 and 0.15 for the two VLMs, respectively, demonstrating that complementary OCR features deliver consistent gains without depending on a particular foundation model.

To reduce development costs while retaining access to high-performance foundation models, the system freezes the VLM and trains only the low-overhead classifier. In production, a worldwide A/B experiment that adjusted the visibility of low-quality A+ Content based on the model’s quality decisions produced a statistically meaningful improvement in Ordered Product Sales (OPS). Beyond aligning closely with expert judgment, the integrated system provides a quality signal that can support customer-experience and business decisions at scale.

Implementation on Amazon SageMaker AI

This section describes how the architecture is implemented end-to-end on Amazon SageMaker AI. Each stage of the pipeline from content rendering and expert annotation through VLM scoring, OCR extraction, feature aggregation, classifier training, SHAP-based explainability, and production monitoring maps to a managed SageMaker AI capability. This design keeps the operational overhead low. The following steps walk through how each component is deployed, connected, and maintained in production.

1. Content snapshot rendering and data ingestion: The complete A+ Content experience is rendered, capturing how customers actually see the page.

SageMaker Processing Jobs run containerized rendering jobs at scale, decoupling data preparation from training and inference compute.

2. VLM scoring and model hosting: Annotators independently label content using the quality rubric. Their aggregated consensus labels become the training targets. The frozen VLM receives each snapshot plus a rubric prompt and outputs four scores from 0 to 10 (Visual Storytelling, Feature Presentation, A+ Layout, Conversion Optimization), each with a confidence value and rationale. SageMaker AI Inference hosts the VLM with the deployment option that fits the workload:

  • Real-Time Endpoints for synchronous, low-latency scoring of individual listings.
  • Asynchronous Endpoints for large payloads such as high-resolution snapshots, where a slight delay is acceptable.
  • Batch Transform for offline bulk scoring at catalog scale.

These options support automatic scaling, managed infrastructure, and GPU instance selection.

SageMaker Training Jobs can optionally be used to further tune or distill the VLM (for example, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapters, knowledge distillation into a smaller model) if teams want a specialized, lower-latency variant. Avoid this to keep recalibration cost-effective and VLM-agnostic.

3. OCR readability extraction: In parallel, OCR extracts text and bounding-box positions from each snapshot and computes four readability signals: Text Density, Character Density, Spacing, and Overall Readability.

SageMaker JumpStart provides pre-trained, single-action deployable models from its model hub, avoiding the need to source, package, and benchmark models from scratch. Teams select a model, optionally fine-tune it without managing infrastructure using SageMaker Serverless Model Customization on ecommerce content, and deploy directly. SageMaker AI Inference then hosts the chosen OCR model as an endpoint.

4. Feature aggregation and storage:

SageMaker Feature Store provides both online (low-latency inference) and offline (batch training) access to the same features, avoiding training-serving skew. Teams can share features across the organization, so downstream consumers can reuse the same curated features.

5. Classifier training: A CatBoost classifier is trained on the eight-dimensional feature vector against expert annotations to learn non-uniform dimension weights and nonlinear decision boundaries. SageMaker Training Jobs can be used here again. You can register trained models directly to SageMaker Model Registry for versioning, approval workflows, and production deployment.

6. SHAP explainability and recommendations: SageMaker Processing Jobs support Bring Your Own (BYO) processing code, which you can use to derive SHAP values and model explainability metrics.

7. Production monitoring and re-training: In production, ML models naturally degrade over time. Customer aesthetics shift, new A+ module types launch, product categories evolve, and seller behavior changes. The scoring patterns the classifier learned from historical annotations gradually fall out of alignment with what quality means today, leading to silent accuracy erosion if left unchecked. Continuous monitoring closes this gap by detecting when the live data distribution or model predictions have drifted far enough from the training baseline to warrant recalibration.

SageMaker AI ModelOps provides a collection of examples and resources to help you operationalize generative AI and machine learning workloads on SageMaker AI.

SageMaker AIOps provides the tool to track data quality, model quality, and feature-attribution drift. SageMaker Pipelines also automates the re-training workflow end-to-end when drift thresholds are breached.

8. Diffusion-based content generation: Closing the loop, the quality scores and SHAP-derived recommendations condition a diffusion model that generates improved A+ image assets. Rather than leaving sellers to interpret recommendations and create new content from scratch, the system produces ready-to-use visual assets (upgraded lifestyle imagery, rebalanced layouts, or enhanced product shots) that directly address the dimensions SHAP flagged as most negatively contributing. These generated assets and natural-language improvement suggestions are surfaced to sellers, so they can upgrade their listings on amazon.com.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed how to evaluate product detail pages as customers see them by rendering each page as a single snapshot and scoring it with a VLM. We also walked through implementing the system on Amazon SageMaker AI. We built the system around three goals. For adaptability, we keep the VLM fixed and train a CatBoost classifier on its rubric scores, so the system matches expert judgment and can be updated with a short CPU-only job. For performance, we add OCR readability scores that catch dense or poorly spaced text the VLM misses. For explainability, SHAP identifies which features drove each decision, and an LLM turns those results into prioritized recommendations for selling partners.

On 5,478 product detail pages from 10 product categories, the fused model reached 0.94 accuracy and a 0.95 F1 score, 14 and 11 percentage points above the averaged-score baseline. Pages revised using the recommendations improved their quality score by an average of 1.4 points on a scale of 10.

Content quality standards differ across product categories, languages, and marketplaces, and our expert annotations can’t fully represent every context. Next, we plan to evaluate more efficient VLM backbones and inference methods to run the system on a global catalog.

entries.title: Use decision models with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations
entries.summary: Some agent-evaluation questions are narrow and repeatable, and decision models answer exactly that kind of question. This post shows how to connect two decision models, Jev and Strands Decider, to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations through code-based evaluators, and how to validate a decision-model check before you gate a release on it.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Use decision models with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations

Some of the questions you ask when evaluating an agent are narrow and repeatable. Did this response stay on policy? Is this tool call safe to approve? Does this answer match the retrieved context? Decision models answer exactly that kind of question. They take a structured state and a fixed set of allowed answers and return a calibrated probability over them, rather than free-form text whose confidence drifts from run to run. That makes them a strong fit for the scoring step in an agent evaluation, where you want a label and a number you can threshold and trust.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, scores an agent through its entire lifecycle, on demand during development, in batch jobs against stored sessions, and online against production traffic. Alongside 15 built-in evaluators, AgentCore Evaluations supports custom evaluators that you define as either an LLM-as-a-judge or a code-based evaluator. Custom LLM-as-a-judge evaluators apply your instructions and rating scale with a model in Amazon Bedrock. Code-based evaluators run your own logic in an AWS Lambda function, and that logic can call your choice of external system, model, or API, including a decision model.

Decision models suit questions with a fixed set of answers that an informed person could decide at a glance, such as whether the agent refused a request or whether a response stayed on topic. After you validate a question on your own traffic, a decision model can be sufficient for that decision or score, and you can extend the same approach to specific harmfulness or stereotyping categories in your policy. Because both backends can answer several questions about the same state in a single request, you can use them as a screening layer rather than a replacement, running a pass or fail signal across your metrics to select the turns that warrant deeper assessment by the built-in evaluators, whose explanations help you investigate what went wrong.

This post shows how to connect two decision model backends to AgentCore Evaluations through code-based evaluators. The first is Jev, a hosted decision model from TypeSafe. The second is Strands Decider 2B, an open-source decision model you run yourself. By the end of this post, you will know how to convert the AgentCore evaluator input into a decision model request, and the model’s probabilities back into an AgentCore evaluation result. First, though, when should you reach for a custom LLM-as-a-judge evaluator, and when does a decision model fit better? The next section breaks down what a decision model is and the trade-offs involved.

Decision models

A decision model is a small, specialized model trained to select from a fixed set of options and return calibrated confidence scores rather than generating free-form text. A general-purpose large language model (LLM) evaluator produces a score with a rationale. A decision model instead produces a probability distribution over predefined answers. That gives you a direct confidence measure you can threshold, aggregate, and act on programmatically. This makes decision models well-suited for evaluation tasks where the judgment can be stated as a choice among a fixed set of options: “Is this response grounded?” or “Did the agent complete the user’s goal?”

Decision models are most useful when you want a well-calibrated confidence score alongside the label, not just a binary judgment. They are also appropriate when you want to enforce a specific rubric consistently without relying on a general-purpose LLM to interpret it.

Jev, the hosted decision model from TypeSafe, and Strands Decider, an open-source, 2-billion-parameter decision model from the Strands Agents team, both support three types of questions. A 

noul
question poses a yes/no question and returns a probability between 0 (no) and 1 (yes). A 
choice
question asks which of up to 255 options applies, returning the most probable option along with the full distribution and a confidence. A 
score
question asks which of 2 to 10 ordered levels applies, returning a probability-weighted score, the distribution over levels, and a confidence. Many evaluation rubrics fit one of these types. “Is every fact in this response supported by the tool results?” is a yes/no question, and “How helpful was this response, on a four-level rubric?” is a score.

Decision models versus LLM-as-a-judge

The built-in evaluators in AgentCore today use a general-purpose LLM to assess the agent response against a rubric and explain its judgment. This is valuable when the evaluation requires connecting evidence, identifying missing information, or working through a response in depth in tasks where the explanation is as useful as the score. Decision models are not a replacement for LLM evaluators. They’re an addition that the code-based evaluator framework makes possible. Use them for narrow, well-defined checks alongside the built-in evaluators’ broader assessment.

Solution overview

To show how these evaluator types work together, this post builds an end-to-end example of an HR Assistant agent evaluated by deterministic code-based checks, built-in LLM-as-a-judge evaluators, and decision-model evaluators backed by Jev or Strands Decider 2B.

The agent is built with Strands Agents and deployed to AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. It answers employee questions using five tools that return fixed mock data such as paid time off (PTO) balances, PTO requests, HR policies, benefits, and pay stubs. We use fixed data in this code sample to make it straightforward to verify evaluator behavior from LLM-as-a-judge and decision models. When you additionally have ground truth, you can confirm whether each evaluator catches the right failures. This code sample helps you set up the framework for testing decision models compared to LLM-as-a-judge for your own use cases.

Prerequisites

To deploy the sample, you need the following:

  • An AWS account in a Region where AgentCore Evaluations is available. The sample defaults to US West (Oregon).
  • Amazon CloudWatch Transaction Search enabled in the account.
  • Access to a foundation model in Amazon Bedrock.
  • Python 3.12 or later, the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), and Docker.
  • Jev requires a TypeSafe API key. Visit typesafe.ai for access details.
  • Strands Decider requires a host running the Strands Decider server. You can run it locally for testing, or on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) inside your virtual private cloud (VPC) so the Lambda function can reach it.

Seeing it in action

You can find the full code sample in the AgentCore samples GitHub repository. Two Python scripts handle everything:

  • ../utils/deploy.py
    deploys the HR Assistant to AgentCore runtime.
  • evaluate.py
    deploys evaluators, invokes the agent, and runs the evaluation modes.

Running 

evaluate.py
without flags executes five steps:
  • Creates the Lambda execution role (
    AgentCoreLambdaEvaluatorRole
    ).
  • Packages and deploys two deterministic Lambda evaluators: 
    hr-response-length
    (a trace-level evaluator that checks whether the agent’s response stays within length bounds) and 
    hr-fact-checker
    (a session-level evaluator that regex-validates HR facts against the known mock data).
  • Registers both as AgentCore code-based evaluators through the control plane.
  • Runs on-demand evaluation with 
    EvaluationClient
    and 
    OnDemandEvaluationDatasetRunner
    across five labeled scenarios, combining the code-based evaluators with 
    Builtin.Correctness
    , 
    Builtin.Helpfulness
    , and 
    Builtin.ResponseRelevance
    .
  • Creates an online evaluation configuration that continuously scores live sessions at 100 percent sampling.

At this point you have a working evaluation pipeline with deterministic checks and LLM-as-a-judge scoring. Decision-model evaluators are opt-in. You can add them with a flag, and they run alongside the base evaluators with no changes to the existing flow. Using the flags 

--with-jev --jev-secret-arn
deploys 
jev-evaluator
and registers three evaluators: 
JevGroundedness
, 
JevHelpfulness
, and 
JevGoalCompletion
. Using the flag 
--with-decider
deploys 
strands-decider-evaluator
and registers the same three evaluators backed by Strands Decider 2B. Add 
--decider-ec2
to auto-provision the Amazon EC2 instance, security groups, IAM role, and Lambda VPC configuration without manual console steps.

Each decision-model backend contributes three evaluators:

EvaluatorLevelQuestion typeLabelValue
JevGroundedness / DeciderGroundednessTRACE
noul

JevHelpfulness / DeciderHelpfulnessTRACE
score
(4-level)		 Most probable levelExpected level, scaled 0–1
JevGoalCompletion / DeciderGoalCompletionSESSION

(3-way)		 Most probable optionProbability-weighted value

Build the evaluator with decision models

Using the flags 

--with-jev
and 
--with-decider
creates a custom code-based evaluator, where you have complete control of the code you want to run as your evaluator. We create AWS Lambda functions where the decision model is invoked inside an AWS Lambda function and returns a label or a numeric value. This Lambda function is registered as the code-based evaluator in AgentCore Evaluations.

The Lambda that is registered as the evaluator receives OpenTelemetry spans of the agent. The 

spans.py
module normalizes the shapes OpenTelemetry content can arrive in and then formats it appropriately to make the call to the decision model. For trace-level evaluation, only the targeted turn and brief prior history are sent, whereas the full conversation is included for session-level.

The adapter converts the model’s probability distribution into a result that AgentCore evaluation expects. For a 

noul
question, the probability of 
true
becomes the value and the most probable answer becomes the label. For a 
score
question, the value is the probability-weighted expected level scaled to 
[0, 1]
. For a 
choice
question, it is the weighted average of predefined option values.

Validate a decision-model evaluator on your own traffic

When you rewrite a rubric as a decision model question, you’ve created a new measurement rather than a copy of the old one. A reframed rubric often lands stricter or looser than the original intended, and you won’t see that drift until you check it against real sessions. Before you gate a release on a decision-model evaluator, validate it the same way you’d validate any new measurement, against a labeled sample of your own traffic. The goal of this section is to walk you through that validation end to end, so you finish with an evaluator you can threshold with confidence.

The procedure has five steps.

Step 1. Build a labeled sample. Pull a set of stored sessions from your agent’s traffic, with enough coverage of the failures and edge cases you care about. A sample that covers only the happy path tells you nothing about where the evaluator breaks.

Step 2. Get human reference labels. Have three independent labelers score each turn for the property your question measures and take the majority vote as the reference label. Keep track of which turns were unanimous and which were split. Although unanimous turns are the clear-cut cases, the split-vote turns are the valuable ones, because they reveal ambiguity in the rubric itself before the model ever sees it.

Step 3. Run both evaluators on the same inputs. Run the decision-model evaluator and the matching built-in evaluator over those same sessions in a single batch evaluation. Scoring identical inputs is what makes the comparison apples to apples.

Step 4. Read the results through three lenses. With the majority-vote labels and the easy and hard split in hand, you can now answer the three questions that tell you whether the evaluator is ready.

  • Agreement rate: does it match your humans? Measure how often each evaluator agrees with the majority-vote labels, and do it per question, since one question’s accuracy says nothing about another’s. Then break the numbers out by easy (unanimous) and hard (split-vote) cases. An evaluator that stumbles only on the hard cases is behaving a lot like your human labelers did, which is exactly what you want.
  • Calibration: do the confidence scores mean something? Group turns by the evaluator’s reported probability and compare each group’s agreement with the labels. Higher confidence should track higher accuracy. Then check whether easy cases consistently draw higher confidence than hard ones. If they do, the model’s uncertainty is tracking genuine ambiguity, and you can use those groups to pick a decision threshold per evaluator instead of defaulting to 0.5.
  • Disagreement analysis: where and why do they differ? Find the turns where the two evaluators disagree with each other, and check whether those are the same turns your humans found ambiguous. Read them. Most disagreements trace back to the wording of the question, and a revised question clears them up. When the errors cluster in the hard cases, the rubric is the problem rather than the model.

Step 5. Re-run the check when anything changes. Treat this as a repeatable check rather than a one-time gate. Any time you reword a question or move to a new model version, run it again. Each result’s explanation records the model version that produced it, so you know which version a given score came from.

Choosing the best set of evaluators for your agent

The built-in evaluators remain the foundation of broad evaluation strategy in AgentCore Evaluations. They assess the response against a rubric and its supporting context, and explain the judgment so developers can investigate what went wrong. For the HR Assistant, a faithfulness evaluation can identify a claim that contradicts a tool result, whereas a helpfulness evaluation can point out that the agent answered a balance question but left a requested action incomplete.

Faithfulness, helpfulness, and correctness can require connecting evidence, identifying missing information, or working through a solution. The preprint JEV-as-a-Judge: Accept When Confident, Escalate When Unsure describes a related distinction as “reading versus deriving.” A narrow decision-model check can flag a turn for attention, whereas the built-in evaluator provides the broader assessment and reasoning needed to review it. Decision models shine brightest when you treat them as a gate rather than a replacement. The cascade pattern works like this. First, run a fast, calibrated decision model on every turn of every session to get a cheap pass/fail signal. Then invoke a full LLM evaluator only on sessions where the signal falls below your threshold.

CriterionLLM as JudgeDecision Models as Judge
OutputScore + explanationCalibrated probability
Latency2–10 s~hundreds of ms (network)
CustomizableLimited (fixed prompt templates)Question definitions
Best forQualitative nuance, explanationCalibrated judgment

We recommend the following setup:

  • Configure online evaluation with the built-in evaluators you rely on, as the standard measure of quality across your agents.
  • Add decision-model evaluators for domain-specific yes/no and choice questions to the same configuration, along with deterministic code-based evaluators for anything you can compute exactly.
  • Each week, or on whatever schedule suits your release cycle, query the online results for sessions where a decision-model check failed or scored near its threshold, and run batch evaluations on those sessions with the built-in evaluators to get explanations.
  • Gate releases on the built-in evaluators and on the decision-model evaluators you have validated against labeled data, and track how often the two agree.

Clean up

To avoid ongoing charges, run the 

cleanup.py
that deletes the agent hosted on AgentCore runtime, the evaluators and evaluation config, the AWS Lambda functions that are registered as the evaluators, the EC2 instance that hosts the Strands Decider model, AWS Secrets Manager key and the associated log group on CloudWatch.

Conclusion

In this post, you connected two decision models, Jev and Strands Decider, to AgentCore Evaluations using code-based evaluators, and the accompanying code sample gives you a framework for testing those models and seeing where they add value as evaluators. The built-in evaluators remain your baseline. Decision models add narrow, validated checks that come with a measure of certainty you can threshold and act on. The practical path forward is to add decision-model checks alongside the built-in evaluators you already run, measure how often they agree with your reference labels on your own traffic, and expand coverage only once you trust them.

To get started, review the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations documentation, integrate custom evaluators using code-based evaluators and take a deeper look into Strands Decider model. Get started with code samples by deploying the sample evaluators from the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore sample repository.

entries.title: Smart Approvals in Amazon Quick: Human oversight where it matters
entries.summary: Smart Approvals in Amazon Quick reviews eligible agent actions within your existing controls, reducing unnecessary approval prompts while keeping consequential decisions with a person. See how policy sets the boundary, how a classifier reviews actions, and how AWS CloudTrail and Amazon CloudWatch Logs support audit.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Smart Approvals in Amazon Quick: Human oversight where it matters

How should security leaders preserve human oversight as AI agents take on more work? Permissions establish which actions agents can take, but a permitted action can still warrant a person’s judgment. Requiring approval for every step might seem like the safest approach, yet multi-step tasks can produce repeated prompts, even for routine actions. Research on security warnings shows that attention and adherence can decline with repetition. The challenge isn’t to require more approvals, but to preserve attention for decisions that need human review.

Smart Approvals in Amazon Quick addresses this challenge by reviewing eligible actions within your existing controls. It evaluates each proposed action against the user’s request and either approves it automatically or returns it to the user for review. It does this without granting additional permissions or removing required human approvals. Security leaders retain control over which actions must always go to a person, while Smart Approvals is designed to reduce unnecessary interruptions in routine work.

Policy sets the boundary

Quick evaluates each proposed action against Custom Permissions, Quick Guardrails, connector action permissions, and the user’s settings before automated review. Denied actions remain denied, and mandatory human approvals still apply. With Smart Approvals enabled, an action is eligible only when the user’s setting is “Ask each time” and no other control requires human approval. Connector action permissions, configured when a connector is created, can require human approval for specific actions.

Administrators use Custom Permissions to determine who can use Smart Approvals. It’s on by default, but profiles with deny-by-default enabled must explicitly allow it. Users can also turn Smart Approvals off for themselves. That choice applies across conversations and scheduled runs. When it’s off, actions otherwise eligible for automated review require the user’s approval, and no account-level setting can turn it back on for them.

How eligible actions are reviewed

Smart Approvals uses a separate model, the classifier, to evaluate eligible actions against the user’s request and a bounded view of the conversation. It considers what the action does, where data goes, and who it affects. It can consult the user’s knowledge graph, which contains people and working relationships drawn from connected sources. This helps it understand how recipients relate to the user, such as whether a recipient is in the user’s reporting chain. This lookup stays within your Quick account. Quick doesn’t use the content the classifier reviews, including knowledge graph data, to train models or improve the service.

An action can match the request and still warrant human review. Examples include sending content outside the organization or to senior leaders in the user’s reporting chain, changing access, deleting records, or initiating payments. This list isn’t complete, and the classifier also weighs the surrounding context. Reviewing actions against the user’s request adds a check against indirect prompt injection, where instructions in retrieved content attempt to redirect the agent. Quick instructs both the agent and classifier to treat that content as information, not instructions. Model review can still make mistakes, so actions that must always receive human approval, including those that move sensitive data, should require it through connector action permissions.

The classifier provides judgment. The permission service enforces authority. Each automatic approval is single-use, applies only to the exact action and parameters reviewed, and grants no ongoing permission. Quick labels automatic approvals in the conversation. Actions the classifier doesn’t approve return to the user, as do timeouts and other review failures, which never grant automatic approval. These enforcement boundaries limit what an approval authorizes. They don’t establish that the classifier’s judgment was correct.

When an action goes beyond the request

An account manager asks Quick to prepare a quarterly business review brief for AnyCompany using her team’s account notes and last quarter’s email. She then asks Quick to send it to two colleagues she names. Assuming the send is eligible for automated review, Smart Approvals evaluates the proposed action against her request and the available conversation context.

Now suppose an account note says the brief should also go to an all-sales distribution list of about 2,000 people. That would change the audience beyond the recipients she specified, so Smart Approvals is designed to return the proposed send to her for review, where she can decline it. An approval to send to the original recipients can’t be reused for the wider audience.

Audit evidence and investigation

The Quick permission service records permission updates associated with Smart Approvals in AWS CloudTrail in your account. Each event identifies the user, connector, action, and time, and marks the request as associated with Smart Approvals. That marker doesn’t establish that the permission service accepted the grant or that the action ran. Quick also records permission-check verdicts, including denials from connector action permissions, and changes to a user’s Smart Approvals setting.

Investigators can correlate these events by user and time with other Quick activity in CloudTrail and logs delivered through Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Chat logs capture the user’s request, system response, and conversation context. Agent metadata logs record changes to agents. Records from the destination system, such as a sent email or updated ticket, confirm whether the action completed. Together, these sources help reconstruct what happened without treating approval as proof of execution. CloudTrail Event history retains events for 90 days, so configure a trail for longer investigations. Because chat logs can contain sensitive content, restrict access and consider CloudWatch Logs data protection policies to mask sensitive data.

Where to start

Because Smart Approvals is on by default, begin by confirming that actions requiring human approval are configured through connector action permissions. Set up a CloudTrail trail and delivery of chat logs and agent metadata logs to CloudWatch Logs to support investigations. Chat logs capture only activity after delivery is configured, so earlier approvals will lack that conversation context. With approval requirements and logging in place, use Custom Permissions to limit Smart Approvals to a pilot team working on a defined workflow before extending it to other teams.

Before the pilot, define what success looks like: fewer prompts for routine actions, with consequential actions still returning to a person for review. During the pilot, review a sample of automatic approvals and test high-impact cases, such as sending content outside the organization or adding a recipient introduced by a document. Confirm that these cases come back to the user. Confirm that your team can trace each action from approval through execution. Expand to more teams and workflows only when the results meet those criteria, and reassess as actions and policies change.

The measure of effective oversight isn’t how often an agent asks for approval, but whether people retain control over consequential decisions. For security leaders, the case for expanding Smart Approvals should rest on evidence from the pilot. Fewer prompts are valuable when they preserve attention without weakening accountability.

For setup steps, see Smart Approvals in the governance section of the Amazon Quick User Guide.

entries.title: Four layers of context engineering for production AI agents: How Deep Insight applies them in working code
entries.summary: In production AI agents, context management is the real bottleneck. This post presents a four-layer context engineering framework (architecture, prompts, file-based tools, and verification agents), implemented in working code from Deep Insight, an open source multi-agent data analysis solution on the Strands Agents SDK and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Four layers of context engineering for production AI agents: How Deep Insight applies them in working code

When production AI agents handle tasks such as data analysis and report generation, context management can become a major bottleneck. A 200K-token window sounds generous until a real-world task burns through most of it in minutes. Data analysis and report generation leave the agent failing mid-execution, losing accuracy, or driving up costs. A body of published guidance already addresses this, but the individual techniques are easier to read about than to apply. Applied together, they make a measurable difference: in the reference implementation this post walks through, a single write-and-execute tool cuts the tokens each script adds to context by about 95 percent, and loading skills on demand shrinks the system prompt by about 97 percent.

This series organizes that guidance into practices you can apply directly. Anthropic’s engineering posts, together with features built into the Strands Agents SDK, converge on four layers of context engineering: isolate context at the architecture level, control it through prompts, externalize it to the filesystem, and verify it with independent agents and safeguards. In this post (Part 2), you will learn how each layer works and what it looks like in working code. We applied these techniques in Deep Insight, an open source multi-agent data analysis solution built on the Strands Agents SDK and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, which serves as the reference implementation throughout.

Post series

  • Part 1: 5 production challenges in multi-agent systems and how Deep Insight solved them.
  • Part 2: Four layers of context engineering for production AI agents: How Deep Insight applies them in working code.
  • Part 3: Harness engineering in practice: moving Deep Insight from dev to production. (Coming soon!)

The first post defined five core challenges that production multi-agent systems must solve. It introduced how Strands Agents SDK, Amazon Bedrock and Bedrock AgentCore, and AWS Fargate each address different layers of the problem, with code examples. This second post takes the four layers of context engineering practice that sit on top of that architecture and shows each one implemented. The third post guides you through deploying and operating agents in a secure private network on Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC), covering everything needed for real-world operations.

What is context engineering?

Context engineering is the discipline of optimizing the information in a large language model (LLM)’s limited context window so agents perform at their best. Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.5, available on Amazon Bedrock, offers a 200K context window, but complex production tasks quickly exceed it. For example, a seemingly straightforward request like “Analyze sales data and create a DOCX report” runs through several stages: data loading and exploration (5 min), category-based sales analysis (3 min), generating five charts for time-series analysis (10 min), statistical validation (3 min), and final report generation (5 min). Together they consume over 150K tokens across 15 minutes.

Processing such tasks in a single context causes problems: the window overflows mid-task, stale context degrades performance, and errors require re-running the whole pipeline. As context grows, attention to important information drops, and inefficiency raises cost under per-token pricing.

“As the number of tokens in the context window increases, the model’s ability to accurately recall information from that context decreases (Context rot).”

— Anthropic, “Effective Context Engineering for AI Agents” (2025.09)

Context engineering solves exactly these problems, and it is not only a collection of techniques. Spanning architecture design, prompt writing, tool implementation, and verification, it’s a layered discipline where each layer compensates for what the previous ones miss. This post details the four-layer approach you can apply to manage context efficiently.

How to handle tasks that exceed the context window

Anthropic has published several techniques for handling long-horizon tasks. Deep Insight groups these techniques into four layers, with each layer addressing the limitations of the others. The following table sets out the four layers.

LayerPracticeCore PrincipleLimitations
Layer 1: ArchitectureIsolating Context Through Multi-Agent ArchitectureEach agent operates in an independent contextWhen isolation alone is not enough
Layer 2: PromptOutput Control and Behavioral RulesLimiting context intake through promptsWhen prompts alone are not enough
Layer 3: ToolsFile-based Context ExternalizationKeeping heavy content in files outside the contextWhen issues still arise
Layer 4: Verification Agents and SafeguardsIndependent Verification and SafeguardsCatching errors and preventing context overflowFinal line of defense

The sections that follow take each layer in order, stating what the layer prescribes, why the preceding layers alone are insufficient, and how the practice is implemented in Deep Insight.

1. Isolating context through multi-agent architecture

Give each specialized agent its own context window and pass only compressed results to the orchestrator. Deep Insight does this with a hierarchy of Coordinator, Planner, Plan Reviewer, Supervisor, and Tool Agents (Coder, Validator, Reporter, Tracker, Auditor).

With a single agent, all information, from user requests through data exploration, analysis, chart generation, validation, and reporting, accumulates in one context and easily exceeds the window. Giving each agent its own context keeps even the Coder, which uses the most, under 25K tokens total. Each agent receives only what it needs and signals others with a completion notice and brief summary.

The key to isolation is minimizing shared information. Deep Insight uses a Python dictionary, 

shared_state
, that stores only four things:
  • messages
    : The previous agent’s final message (not the full conversation history).
  • clues
    : Compressed summaries collected from each agent.
  • full_plan
    : A checklist generated by Planner and updated by Tracker.
  • history
    : A brief log of agent names and messages.

The clues use a fixed CLUES_FORMAT: instead of each agent’s full conversation (tens of thousands of tokens), only compressed core results are passed.

This pattern is the one recommended in Anthropic’s “How We Built Our Multi-Agent Research System” post, which describes an orchestrator-worker pattern in which a lead agent delegates to specialized subagents, with each agent working only within its own context. You do not need to build it yourself: the agents-as-tools pattern in the Strands Agents SDK provides this isolation at the framework level.

2. Controlling context inflow through prompts

Layer 1 isolation alone is not sufficient: even with independent contexts, an agent that generates long responses inflates the Supervisor’s context. Layer 2 limits each agent’s output through prompts.

For Deep Insight, we use prompts to limit how much information each agent returns to the Supervisor. Three rules do most of the work, as Deep Insight’s prompts show.

“Start with the strongest model and a simple prompt. Then incrementally add specific instructions based on actually observed failure cases.”

— Anthropic, “Effective Context Engineering for AI Agents” (2025.09)

Implementation detail 2-1: Explicit per-agent output token budgets

Each agent’s prompt specifies a maximum response token count, preventing long responses that pollute the Supervisor’s context.

AgentOutput Token BudgetReason
Coder1,000–1,500 tokensAnalysis code is saved to files, so the agent returns only a summary of state, completed tasks, and insights
Validator800 tokensValidation results are saved to 
citations.json
. The agent returns only a summary
Reporter1,000 tokensThe agent generates the report as a DOCX file and returns only a summary of the result

Anthropic’s ” Writing Effective Tools for Agents” post suggests giving tools a CONCISE or DETAILED response option for context efficiency. Apply the same idea one level up, in each agent’s system prompt. In Deep Insight, all agents share one standardized format:

Implementation detail 2-2: Self-contained code philosophy

The Coder agent’s prompt explicitly states “variables do not persist between scripts.” Every script must include all necessary imports and load data directly. The prompt provides both incorrect and correct examples:

The reason this rule relates to context engineering is that referencing variables from previous scripts requires the agent to “remember” prior conversations, which means past code must remain in context. The self-contained principle means past code can be safely removed from context.

Implementation detail 2-3: Supervisor’s section completion rule

The Supervisor’s prompt includes the rule “Do not move to the next agent until all checklist items in the current agent’s section are marked 

[x]
.” We express this rule in the prompt because deciding whether the Coder’s work is complete requires the Supervisor to interpret the plan using information from the Tracker’s updates. This judgment is difficult to express in code alone.

3. “Only pointers in context, actual data in files”

Layer 1 isolates context between agents, and Layer 2 limits output within agents. But when the Coder agent generates 100 lines of Python code, that code itself enters the context. Even with “respond briefly” prompt instructions, some code can’t be written briefly. Layer 3 uses tool design to move heavy content outside the context, into the filesystem. Four techniques carry most of the benefit, as the following implementation details show.

Implementation detail 3-1: Moving code outside context with Write and Execute Tool

The Coder reads the analysis plan, writes Python, and executes it to generate visualizations. But when the code gets long, the conventional approach (separate file-write and execute tools) adds 100 lines directly to context per script, accumulating over 1,000 lines.

The fix is to collapse the two steps into a single tool, so the code never enters context as a message. Deep Insight’s Coder agent uses one 

write_and_execute_tool
for this.

Here’s part of the write_and_execute_tool. After writing and executing the file, it returns only a summary: “Wrote 105 lines, execution successful, completed analysis of five categories.” The code stays in the file and about three lines of summary remain in context. Based on this example, that saves about 95 percent of the tokens.

“Server-side filtering: filtering data at the execution layer before it reaches context, 98.7% token reduction (150K to 2K).”

— Anthropic, “Code Execution with MCP” (2025.11)

Implementation detail 3-2: Reusing common logic as modules in the Coder agent

Common modules get reused across analyses. Rather than regenerating them each time, define frequently-used functions as a module once and import them, which prevents token waste and context duplication.

Without this, defining functions like to_python_type() or track_calculation() in every analysis produces 200–300 lines of duplicate code across 10 analyses. Deep Insight generates a module called 

coder_analysis_utils.py
before the first task. It includes functions for converting numpy types, tracking calculation metadata, and saving to JSON. Subsequent analyses import it, replacing 20–30 regenerated lines with two import lines, which saves tokens and improves consistency and debugging.

Implementation detail 3-3: Saving and sharing analysis results through structured note-taking

We use structured note-taking to share detailed analysis results without passing them through each agent’s context. Deep Insight stores these results in a file called 

all_results.txt
, which is then read by agents as needed.

For example, the Coder agent appends results to 

all_results.txt
after each analysis task:

The Coder records detailed results in this file after each analysis, and the Reporter reads it when writing the final report. Other agents collaborate through all_results.txt the same way.

Without note-taking, the Coder passes detailed results to the Supervisor after every task, accumulating in its context. With note-taking, only an approximately 30-token message like “Category sales analysis complete, 3 key insights found, detailed results saved to all_results.txt” is passed, and the Reporter reads the file when needed.

The pattern generalizes beyond a single file. The filesystem itself can serve as the inter-agent communication bus, as it does in Deep Insight:

File nameProducerConsumerRole
all_results.txtCoderReporterCumulative log of analysis results
calculation_metadata.json

citations.json
